title: The Geographic Determinants of Housing Supply
research_question: To what extent do predetermined geographic features such as oceans, lakes, wetlands, and steep-sloped terrain shape contemporaneous patterns of urban growth, housing prices, and the responsiveness of housing quantities to demand shocks across U.S. metropolitan areas? How do these physical land constraints interact with local land-use regulations, and are such regulations themselves shaped by prior housing prices, demographic growth, and natural land scarcity?
data_description: The author constructs a novel measure of undevelopable land for U.S. metropolitan areas using satellite-based geographic information system (GIS) data. Terrain elevation comes from the USGS Digital Elevation Model at 90-meter resolution, used to compute the share of land with slopes above 15% within a 50-km radius of each metropolitan central city. The 1992 USGS National Land Cover Dataset (30m resolution) provides shares of wetlands, lakes, rivers, and other internal water bodies, and digital contour maps capture area lost to oceans and the Great Lakes. Regulatory stringency is measured using the 2005 Wharton Residential Land Use Regulatory Index aggregated from municipalities to MSAs. Housing prices, housing units, population, income, education, immigration, and industrial composition come from decennial U.S. Censuses (1970–2000), supplemented by Freddie Mac repeat-sales indices, Census of Governments data on local expenditures, religious adherence data, and amenity measures (hours of sun, tourist visits). The unit of observation is the MSA, with a primary sample of 269 metropolitan areas.
institutional_context: Housing markets in U.S. metropolitan areas vary enormously in price levels and growth, and a longstanding debate concerns whether such variation reflects man-made restrictions on building or genuine physical scarcity of developable land. Coastal metros like Miami, San Francisco, Los Angeles, New York, Boston, and San Diego are bounded by oceans, mountains, and wetlands that physically preclude construction on large fractions of nearby land, while interior metros like Atlanta, Houston, Dallas, and Indianapolis sit on largely flat, dry terrain. At the same time, local jurisdictions adopt zoning, growth controls, and project-approval practices of varying stringency, often shaped by homeowner political incentives (the 'homevoter' logic), fiscal zoning, nuisance concerns, and local preferences toward government activism (proxied by religious composition and protective-inspection spending). The interplay between immutable topography and politically chosen regulation defines the supply environment that determines how national demand shocks—from immigration, industrial restructuring, and amenity-driven migration—translate into prices versus quantities.
